analysis.one_liner: Lets adults buy hearing aids for mild-to-moderate hearing loss over the counter, no prescription needed.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: after referral, it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Hearing aids for mild-to-moderate hearing loss currently require a visit with a licensed professional before they can be sold. This bill would direct the FDA to create an over-the-counter category for adults 18 and older, sold in person, by mail, or online, with federal rules covering safety, volume limits, and labeling. It would also stop states from adding extra requirements, like a mandatory prescription, that get in the way of those sales.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss who find professionally fitted hearing aids too expensive. Traditional hearing aids often cost thousands of dollars and require multiple clinic visits; an over-the-counter category would allow self-fitted, lower-cost devices sold online or in stores, with FDA rules on safety, output limits, and labeling.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to create an over-the-counter hearing aid category that adults can buy without the involvement of a licensed professional, through in-person, mail, or online sales.
Directs the FDA to write regulations ensuring safety and effectiveness, setting output limits, and requiring labeling that tells users how to report problems and when to see a physician.
Bars state and local governments from imposing requirements on these devices that go beyond the FDA rules, including state mandates for a prescription or professional supervision to buy one.

Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to finalize 2013 draft guidance clarifying which products are regulated medical devices and which are simple sound amplifiers, reducing confusion for shoppers.

analysis.who_pays: Hearing aid dispensers and audiologists lose revenue from the mandatory evaluation-and-fitting visit, and established hearing aid makers lose the protection of a sales channel where devices commonly cost thousands of dollars. Consumers bear no direct cost, though some may skip a medical evaluation their hearing problem actually called for.

drawbacks.text: Without a professional exam, some buyers could treat hearing loss with an amplifier when the real cause needs medical care; the bill addresses this only through labeling that flags contraindications and advises seeing a physician promptly.
Safety rests on FDA rulemaking the bill gives up to three years to propose; weak final rules on output limits could leave users exposed to devices that do more harm than good.
The bill overrides state and local rules on hearing products that are stricter than the FDA's, taking away tougher consumer protections some states might have chosen to keep.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and the costs modest. Hearing loss affects a large share of older adults, and the gatekeeping requirement adds both price and delay for devices that are essentially miniaturized electronics. The genuine risk — that someone self-treats a condition that needed a doctor — is a real objection, but the bill's labeling and physician-consult requirements are the standard way regulators have handled comparable products. On balance this is a well-designed consumer access bill, not a badly designed one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to the Health Subcommittee three days later, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III introduced the bill on March 21, 2017, joined on the introduction by Rep. Buddy Carter of Georgia and Rep. Marsha Blackburn, a Democrat and two Republicans.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and to the committee's Health Subcommittee on March 24, 2017.
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill — 4 Republicans and 10 Democrats — but no further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For the life of this Congress, hearing aid dispensers, audiologists, and incumbent manufacturers kept the prescription-and-fitting sales model and its prices, because the bill that would have opened the market never left committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hearing dispensers and incumbent makers, for now

industries.industry: Audiologists and licensed hearing aid dispensers
industries.note: The bill removes the legal requirement that a licensed professional be involved in selling hearing aids to people with mild-to-moderate loss, ending the mandatory evaluation-and-fitting appointments that generate much of this profession's revenue. Consumers would no longer have to pay for that gatekeeping to get a device.

They would lose the protection of a sales channel where devices commonly sell for thousands of dollars through clinics, but they also gain the option to sell into a new mass-market category. Their long-standing business model depended on the professional-dispensing requirement this bill repeals.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics makers and big-box and online retailers
industries.note: A federally defined over-the-counter category, sellable by mail and online without a licensed intermediary, opens a large new consumer market for electronics companies and retailers. Their gain comes directly from lower prices for shoppers.
